text: To be beset by something is to be surrounded and troubled by it from several sides at once — not one problem, but problems arriving from every direction. It almost always goes with difficulties, and it hints that you are struggling under them. The writer uses it to say Japan's tea industry has three troubles hitting it together: farmers growing old, too few workers, and Chinese competition.

You probably know a dwarf as a short character in a story, but as a verb, to dwarf something is to be so much bigger than it that it looks tiny next to you. Nothing actually shrinks; it only looks small by comparison. China grows 70% of the world's matcha, so much more than Japan that Japan's crop looks small beside it.

Cultivation is the work of growing plants on purpose: preparing soil, planting, watering, feeding and harvesting. The word also covers how you grow something, so two farms can use quite different cultivation methods on the very same plant. Matcha tea has to be grown in shade, which is why a farmer set up for ordinary tea cannot simply switch over.

Here stretch has nothing to do with pulling something longer or warming up before a game. When a thing stretches across a space, it covers or extends over all of it. The rows of tea bushes stretch across the field, meaning they reach from one side of it to the other.

To inherit something is to receive it from a family member who has died or stopped working, usually passed down by law. People inherit money, houses, farms and businesses. Nishi Toshimi inherited his family tea farm, so it came down to him rather than being bought.

A decade is a period of ten years. Two decades ago means twenty years ago, and a decade earlier means ten years before the moment being described. Writers use it to talk about long stretches of time without listing exact dates.

An industry is not a single factory. It means all the companies and workers who make one kind of thing, taken together — the car industry, the music industry, and here Japan's tea industry. So an industry in poor shape means the whole business of growing and selling tea is struggling, not one farm.

To go or head downhill means to get steadily worse, and it has nothing to do with real hills or slopes. People say it about health, grades, a team's season or a business. Japan's tea industry was heading downhill when prices were dropping and sales were shrinking.

A boom is not a loud noise here. In business a boom is a sudden stretch of time when something sells far more than before and prices rise — the opposite of a slump. The matcha boom means buyers all over the world started wanting matcha at once, and Japanese tea farms became busy and profitable again.

Exports are goods a country sells to buyers in other countries; imports are what it buys in from them. Governments track the totals closely, because selling abroad brings money home. Japan's green-tea exports reached 12,600 tonnes, meaning that much tea left Japan for customers overseas.

A tonne is a metric unit of weight: 1,000 kilograms, which is about 2,200 pounds, a little more than an American ton. The spelling with two n's and an e is the metric one used in most of the world. Giving the harvest as 12,600 tonnes measures it by weight rather than by counting leaves.

To surge is to rise quickly and strongly, the way a wave pushes up a beach. Used about numbers, it means a sharp climb in a short time. Tea prices surged, so they did not drift up slowly — they jumped.

Something coveted is wanted badly by a great many people, enough that they envy whoever has it. You hear it about trophies, jobs and rare collectables. Uji matcha from near Kyoto is coveted, meaning tea drinkers prize it and will pay extra for it.

A household name is a name almost everybody recognizes — familiar enough that you would hear it in any home. Nike, Google and Toyota are household names. Kagoshima is barely a household name, so even in Japan most people would not think of it when they think of tea.

A fortune can mean a huge pile of money, but in the plural, somebody's fortunes means how well or badly they are doing overall. A team's fortunes can improve after a new coach arrives. The boom transformed Kagoshima's fortunes, so the area went from struggling to thriving.

Kagoshima is a region at the southern tip of Japan, warm enough to grow tea well. It was never famous for tea, yet by 2024 it had become Japan's biggest tea producer. The name covers both a city and the wider prefecture, which is something like a state or county, around it.
Kyushu is the southernmost of Japan's four main islands. Japan is a chain of islands, and Kyushu sits at the warm end, which suits crops like tea. Kagoshima is on Kyushu.

Kyoto is a historic Japanese city that served as the country's capital for more than a thousand years, and it is home to many of Japan's oldest traditions, including the tea ceremony. Tea grown nearby, in the Uji area, has the best-known reputation in Japan.

Uji is a small city just outside Kyoto, famous for centuries as the source of Japan's finest matcha. Uji matcha works rather like a brand name: it tells a buyer where the tea was grown and signals high quality.
Shizuoka is a region in central Japan, near Mount Fuji, and has long been the country's traditional tea-growing area. It specializes in leaves for brewed green tea rather than in powder for matcha.

Nishi Toshimi is the Kagoshima tea farmer this article follows. He took over his family farm about twenty years ago, when the business was failing, and has lived to see the matcha boom rescue it. Japanese names are usually written family name first, so Nishi is his family name — which is why the writer later calls him Mr Nishi.

Matcha is green tea that has been dried and ground into a fine powder, then whisked into water or milk so that you swallow the whole leaf. That makes the taste stronger and the color a bright green, and it is why matcha shows up in lattes, ice cream and cake. With ordinary green tea the leaves are soaked and then thrown away.

Tencha is the particular tea leaf that gets ground into matcha powder. It is grown in shade and processed differently from ordinary tea leaves, so not every tea farm is able to produce it. Kagoshima now grows about 40% of Japan's tencha.

Sencha is the everyday Japanese green tea, made by soaking whole leaves in hot water and then removing them. It is what most people in Japan actually drink at home, even while the rest of the world is buying matcha powder.

To brew a drink is to soak leaves or ground beans in hot water so the flavor passes into the water, then take the solids out. Tea and coffee are both brewed that way. The article contrasts brewing tea leaves with using matcha powder, where the ground leaf stays in the cup.

When a powder dissolves, its tiny pieces spread out through a liquid until the mixture looks even all the way through, the way sugar disappears into water. The powder has not gone anywhere; it is still in the cup. Matcha powder is whisked in and stays in the drink, instead of being soaked and then removed like tea leaves.

In everyday speech, to demand is to insist on something, but in business demand is a quantity: how much of a thing people want to buy at a given time. Strong demand pushes prices up and keeps sellers busy. Global demand for matcha is rising while demand at home in Japan keeps falling.

To crave something is to want it intensely, almost like a physical hunger — the feeling you get about a snack you cannot stop thinking about. It is far stronger than simply liking something. Saying the world craves matcha pictures buyers everywhere eager for it.

Consumption means the total amount of something that gets used up, eaten or drunk. Researchers often measure it per person so that countries of different sizes can be compared fairly. Japanese tea consumption fell from 527 grams per person in 1970 to 233 in 2024, so the average person now drinks less than half as much.

Per person means for each single person: you take a total and divide it by how many people there are. It makes a huge country and a small one comparable, since a country can use more tea in total simply because more people live there. So 527 grams per person describes the average Japanese tea drinker, not the whole country's supply.

A successor is the person who takes over a job, role or title after somebody leaves it — the next principal, the next king, the next owner of a shop. To retire without a successor is to stop with nobody lined up to continue the work. That is why Japanese tea fields are vanishing: farmers stop and no younger farmer steps in.

Usually devoted describes a person who is loyal and loving, like a devoted fan. But land or time devoted to something simply means set aside for that purpose and used for nothing else. The area devoted to tea cultivation is the land being used to grow tea, and it shrank by 31%.

Ageing means growing older; British writers spell it with an e, while Americans usually write aging. Calling a group ageing says the people in it are getting older on average, with few younger ones joining. Japan's tea farmers are ageing, so many of them are near the end of their working lives.

Labour is the British spelling of labor, meaning work, or the people who do the work. A labour shortage is when there is more work needing to be done than there are workers available to do it, so some of it goes undone no matter how good business is. Japanese tea farms cannot find enough hands even during a boom.

To lean into something means to commit to it and push harder at it, not to tip your body toward it. People say it about a skill, a trend or a plan. Not all farmers can lean into the matcha boom, meaning they cannot shift their farms over to take advantage of it.

Shading a plant means covering it so that less sunlight reaches it, usually with cloth or screens. Growers do this on purpose: tea leaves kept in shade build up more of the substances that give matcha its deep green color and sweeter taste. It takes extra work and extra equipment, which is part of why not every farm grows tencha.

Facilities are buildings and equipment set up for one particular job — a sports facility, a research facility, or here the sheds and machines needed to turn tea leaves into matcha powder. Calling them costly facilities means a farmer would have to spend a great deal of money before producing any matcha at all.

A producer is not only somebody who makes films. In business a producer is any person, company or country that makes or grows something in order to sell it. Shizuoka is a producer of brewed green tea, and Japanese producers are the farms and firms making matcha.

The high end of a market is the expensive, best-quality part of it, where buyers pay more for something finer; the low end is the cheap, plain part. Phones, bicycles and chocolate all have a high end. Saying Japan's future lies at the high end means Japan should aim to sell the finest matcha rather than the most matcha.

A sophisticated machine is complicated and advanced, but a sophisticated taste or flavor means subtle and complex — many layers rather than one blunt note. Japanese producers claim their matcha is more sophisticated than China's, so they mean it tastes more refined, not that it is high-tech.

The Japanese tea ceremony is a formal, centuries-old way of preparing and serving matcha, with set movements, special bowls and careful manners. It is treated as an art form and studied for years. Because the ceremony is built around matcha, Japan's claim to understand matcha best rests partly on it.

Champagne is a region in northern France, and by law only sparkling wine made there may be sold under that name; the identical drink made anywhere else has to be called sparkling wine. Protecting a place name this way lets the producers inside it charge more. Mr Nishi wants Japanese matcha protected in the same fashion, so that nobody else may use the name.

To lose out is to miss a benefit that somebody else ends up getting, rather than to lose a game outright. You lose out on a chance, a prize or a sale. Mr Nishi warns that Japan will lose out if it does not protect its name, meaning China would take the profitable part of the matcha business.
